title: Muktinath for Hindu and Buddhist pilgrims
meta_description: Muktinath pilgrimage guide: how to reach the temple by air, road or helicopter, the 108 spouts and Jwala Mai, altitude, seasons, permits and where to stay.
summary: Muktinath, at about 3,710 m in Lower Mustang, is holy to Hindus as Mukti Kshetra and to Buddhists as Chumig Gyatsa. Most pilgrims fly Pokhara to Jomsom and drive 1.5 hours up, or drive from Pokhara in one to two days. Sleep at Kagbeni or Ranipauwa, bathe at dawn, and take altitude seriously.

sections.heading: One shrine, two faiths
paras: Muktinath stands in a grove of poplars at the head of the Jhong valley, above the village of Ranipauwa, with the bare slopes of the Thorong La rising behind. For Hindus it is Mukti Kshetra, the place of liberation, sacred to Vishnu as Shri Muktinarayan. It is counted among the 108 Divya Desam, the Vishnu shrines praised by the Tamil Alvar poets, and many Vaishnava pilgrims from South India make the long journey here. The Kali Gandaki below is the source of Shaligram stones, the black fossils worshipped as forms of Vishnu.

For Tibetan Buddhists the same place is Chumig Gyatsa, the Hundred Springs. Tradition says Guru Rinpoche, Padmasambhava, meditated here on his way to Tibet, and the site is honoured as a place of the dakinis, female wisdom beings. Buddhist nuns help tend the shrines, and both Hindu and Buddhist pilgrims walk the same paths, bathe in the same water and bow at the same flame. Few places show so clearly how the two traditions share sacred ground in Nepal.

sections.heading: What you will find in the compound
paras: The temple compound is small and can be seen in an hour, though most pilgrims stay much longer. Enter through the gate at the top of the path from Ranipauwa and you will pass, in turn, the main sites below. Shoes come off near the main temple; your guide will show you where to leave them.
list: The main temple of Shri Muktinarayan, a pagoda-style shrine housing the image of Vishnu
The Muktidhara, 108 water spouts shaped like bull heads in a semicircle behind the temple, fed by the springs above
Two small kunds, or ponds, in front of the temple, where pilgrims dip after bathing at the spouts
Jwala Mai, called Mebar Lhakhang by Buddhists, where a small flame of natural gas burns beside a trickle of spring water
Buddhist gompas and chortens around the compound, with prayer wheels and butter lamps

sections.heading: How to get there
paras: Muktinath lies a short drive north-east of Jomsom, the district headquarters and airport for Mustang, up the side valley that leaves the Kali Gandaki at Kagbeni. There are three main ways to reach it from Pokhara, which is itself 25 minutes by air or 6 to 8 hours by road from Kathmandu. Times below are typical in dry weather.

sections.heading: Altitude and health
paras: The temple stands at about 3,710 m, high enough for altitude sickness. Pilgrims who fly from Pokhara at 820 m to Jomsom and drive straight up to the temple in one morning are the ones most likely to suffer: headache, nausea, dizziness and breathlessness. In rare cases it becomes serious. The safest approach is to sleep a night at Jomsom (2,720 m) or Kagbeni (2,810 m) first, then go up to Muktinath the next day and, ideally, sleep at Ranipauwa (3,700 m) so you can visit at dawn.

Walk slowly on the path to the temple, which climbs for 15 to 20 minutes from Ranipauwa. Drink plenty of water, avoid alcohol and smoking, and do not exert yourself running repeatedly under the spouts. Elderly pilgrims and anyone with heart, lung or blood pressure problems should consult a doctor before travelling. Ponies, and porters with baskets, can carry those who cannot walk. If someone feels unwell, the answer is to go down; Jomsom is just 1.5 hours away by jeep.

sections.heading: Rituals and offerings
paras: Most Hindu pilgrims follow a simple sequence. They bathe under all 108 spouts, moving along the line from one end to the other, then dip in the two kunds, which are believed to wash away the weight of past deeds. Then they take darshan of Shri Muktinarayan in the main temple, offer flowers, sweets and coins, and visit Jwala Mai to see fire burning beside water. Many fill small bottles with water from the spouts to take home.

On the way to or from the temple, many families stop at Kagbeni, at the confluence of the Kali Gandaki and Jhong rivers, to perform shraddha or pinda daan for their ancestors with a local priest. Others search the Kali Gandaki riverbed for Shaligram stones, or buy them from stalls in Jomsom and Ranipauwa. Buddhist pilgrims light butter lamps, turn prayer wheels and walk clockwise around the compound. Whatever your faith, ask before photographing people at prayer or bathing.

sections.heading: When to go
paras: The temple is open all year. March to May and September to November bring the most reliable flights, clear skies and comfortable days, and the most pilgrims. December to February is very cold, and snow can fall at Muktinath, but the road and flights usually operate and the compound is quiet. June to September is the hardest time: Mustang itself stays fairly dry, but landslides on the road below Jomsom and cloud in the gorge cause long delays.

Bathe early. The water from the spouts is close to freezing all year, and the valley wind rises from late morning, making a wet, cold pilgrim very uncomfortable. At dawn the light is soft, the compound calm and the priests and nuns are beginning the day's worship.

sections.heading: Villages worth a stop on the way
paras: Most pilgrims rush past the villages between Jomsom and Muktinath, which is a pity, because they add depth to the journey and give the body time to adjust. Kagbeni, at the river confluence, is a fortified village of narrow lanes, tunnels and an old red monastery, with clay guardian figures at its edges to keep harm away. Jharkot, on the road below Ranipauwa, is a cluster of old houses and a monastery around the ruins of a fort, with wide views back down the valley.

If you have an extra half day, walk down from Muktinath to Lubra by the Panda Khola, a quiet village where people follow Bon, the old religion of Tibet, and continue to Jomsom. It is a three to four hour walk, mostly downhill, and a gentle way to end a pilgrimage among people who have kept their own faith alive for centuries.

sections.heading: Practical notes for the journey
paras: Ranipauwa, below the temple, has many lodges and simple hotels, some with attached bathrooms and hot water, and most serve vegetarian food. Jomsom has more choice and an ATM, but carry enough Nepali rupees for the trip, since cards are rarely accepted. Mobile signal is generally available in Jomsom, Kagbeni and Ranipauwa.

Muktinath lies inside the Annapurna Conservation Area, so foreign visitors need its permit: NPR 3,000, or NPR 1,000 for SAARC nationals including Indians. Under rules introduced in 2023, foreigners are expected to travel with a licensed guide. Indian citizens do not need a visa for Nepal but should carry a passport or voter ID. Check current status before you travel.
list: A full change of clothes and a quick-dry towel for the bath
Warm jacket, hat and gloves, even in May and October
Sunglasses, sunscreen and a scarf against wind and dust
A small bottle for holy water and a bag for offerings
Any regular medicines, plus something for headache and stomach upsets

faqs.a: The Muktinath temple stands at about 3,710 m above sea level, with the village of Ranipauwa just below it at about 3,700 m. That is high enough for altitude sickness, especially if you arrive quickly from Pokhara at 820 m. Spend a night at Jomsom or Kagbeni first, walk slowly and drink plenty of water.

faqs.q: How many days are needed for a Muktinath trip?
faqs.a: From Kathmandu, allow at least four nights by air: Pokhara, Kagbeni or Jomsom, Ranipauwa, and Jomsom again, then fly out. By road from Pokhara, five to six nights is comfortable. A helicopter can do it in a day, but it leaves almost no time to adjust to the altitude or to pray unhurriedly.

faqs.q: Why does Muktinath have 108 water spouts?
faqs.a: The 108 spouts, called Muktidhara, are arranged in a semicircle behind the main Vishnu temple, each shaped like a bull's head, and are fed by springs above. The number 108 is sacred in both Hinduism and Buddhism. Hindus believe bathing under all of them purifies the soul and helps bring liberation, or mukti.

faqs.q: What is Jwala Mai at Muktinath?
faqs.a: Jwala Mai is a small shrine in the Muktinath compound where a flame of natural gas burns beside a spring, so fire and water appear together. Hindus honour it as a form of the goddess, and Buddhists call it Mebar Lhakhang. Both see the meeting of fire, water and earth as a sign of the place's sanctity.

faqs.q: Do Indians need a permit for Muktinath?
faqs.a: Yes. Muktinath lies in the Annapurna Conservation Area, and Indian citizens pay the SAARC rate for its permit, NPR 1,000. Indians do not need a visa for Nepal but should carry a passport or voter ID. No restricted-area permit is needed for Muktinath itself. Check current status before you travel, as rules are revised.

Yes, many do. The flight to Jomsom and a jeep to Ranipauwa avoid long walks, and ponies or porters can carry people up the final path to the temple. The main concern is altitude, so a night lower down first is important. Anyone with heart, lung or blood pressure conditions should see a doctor before travelling.

faqs.q: What is the best time to visit Muktinath?
faqs.a: March to May and September to November are best, with clear weather and reliable flights. Winter is very cold, with occasional snow, but the temple is open and quiet. The monsoon months, June to September, bring landslides on the road below Jomsom and frequent flight delays, so allow extra days if you travel then.

faqs.q: Can I find Shaligram stones near Muktinath?
faqs.a: Shaligrams are found mainly in the bed of the Kali Gandaki, especially around Kagbeni and further north, rather than at the temple itself. With patience you may find small ones on the riverbed when the water is low. They are also sold at stalls in Jomsom, Kagbeni and Ranipauwa. Hindus worship them as natural forms of Vishnu.

faqs.q: Where should I stay at Muktinath?
faqs.a: Ranipauwa, the village below the temple, has many lodges and hotels for pilgrims, from basic rooms to simple hotels with attached bathrooms. Staying there lets you visit the temple at dawn. If you are worried about altitude, sleep lower at Kagbeni or Jomsom and visit Muktinath as a day trip, about 1 to 1.5 hours each way by jeep.
